title: Wide Field Imager view of a Milky Way look-alike, NGC 6744
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 6744, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope
celestial: NGC 6744 · constellation Pavo · about 30 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This is NGC 6744, a large, nearby spiral galaxy photographed with the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope's Wide Field Imager, at La Silla in Chile. It is of special interest because it resembles our own galaxy.

We can never photograph the Milky Way from outside, because we live inside its disc. NGC 6744 is similar enough that this image works almost like a picture postcard of home, as if someone had mailed us a snapshot of our galaxy from far out in intergalactic space.

A spiral galaxy like this one is a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust, with arms winding out from a brighter center. Four exposures went into it. Three captured blue, yellow-green and red light, and a fourth isolated the glow of hydrogen gas, which traces regions where new stars are forming.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (21.07 x 17.74 arcminutes) and distance (30 million light years), the frame spans roughly 184,000 × 155,000 light-years. Its light set out about 30 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope. Blue light is shown as blue, yellow-green as green, red as orange, and the glow of hydrogen gas as red.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see this way by eye, and the long exposures gather much more light than an eye can.

explore: NGC 6744 lies about 30 million light-years away in the southern constellation Pavo, the Peacock.
alt: A large spiral galaxy with arms winding out from a bright center.
